title: Pilgrimage
hook: traveling to a holy place as prayer

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessings: cars, dogs, throats, fields, a new apartment that still smelled of paint. Your line was everything can be blessed. What did you give thanks for before you used it? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

Two friends are walking out of Jerusalem on a Sunday, heading for a village called Emmaus. Their feet hurt and their hearts hurt worse. The man they had hoped in has been crucified, and now there are strange reports of an empty tomb. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about. They stop, faces sad, and tell him everything. He listens. Then, as they keep walking, he opens the scriptures to them, step after step. They don't know who he is. They only know they don't want the road to end. Today's word is a journey like that one: a walk that turns into a prayer.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS LEAVING JERUSALEM.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `THEY DON'T WANT THE ROAD TO END.`

segments.voice: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place, made as prayer. Not tourism with a church stop. The trip itself is the point. First, the pilgrim habit runs through scripture. Luke's Gospel says Jesus's parents went up to Jerusalem every year for the Passover, and that when he was twelve they took him along. Tradition hears some of the Psalms as songs for pilgrims going up to the Temple. One opens, in the Douay-Rheims, "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." Second, what the Catechism says pilgrimages are for. It says they evoke our earthly journey toward heaven, and that they are traditionally special times for renewal in prayer. So the road is a picture. Every pilgrim is acting out, with their legs, what the Catechism says about the whole of life: we're on the way, not yet home. Third, back to Emmaus, because that walk shows what can happen on the road. At the village, the two friends press the stranger to stay, since evening is coming. At table he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it, and their eyes are opened. He vanishes. And they say to each other, "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way?" In the way. On the road, before they knew. Last, the Church calls herself a pilgrim. The Second Vatican Council speaks of the pilgrim Church on earth. A pilgrimage to a shrine is a small version of that bigger walk, done on purpose, with tired feet.
screen: `JESUS'S FAMILY WENT UP EACH YEAR.` · `A PICTURE OF THE WHOLE JOURNEY.` · `OUR HEART BURNING, IN THE WAY.` · `A PILGRIM CHURCH.` · then, large: `WE SHALL GO INTO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a walk to a church. Not a drive, if you can manage it. Settle, and breathe. Picture the nearest church you could reach on foot. Picture leaving your door. Which street first? What will you pass? A bakery, a school, a bus stop full of people. Decide now that the walk itself will be the prayer: no headphones, no hurry. If you pray, you might say a Hail Mary at each corner, or simply walk in silence. If you don't, just notice every step. When you arrive, sit for a minute, then walk home. The bell holds the time.
Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, made as prayer, in which the road itself becomes part of the prayer. Today's word.
Your line: the road is the prayer. Today, walk to a church, even a short way, and let the walk count as much as the arrival. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to shrines near and far, often in parish groups, with Mass, confession and prayer along the way; some walk the whole route on foot.

notes: Luke 2:41–42 paraphrased: parents went to Jerusalem every year at Passover; when he was twelve they went up. The 'twelve' is stated in the cited text.
'Songs that pilgrims sang going up to the Temple' refers to the Gradual Psalms / Songs of Ascents (DR Psalms 119–133); the pilgrim use is traditional. Confirm the phrasing.
Douay-Rheims wording of Psalm 121:1 and Luke 24:32: confirm.
CCC 2691 paraphrased; Lumen Gentium chapter 7 on the pilgrim Church paraphrased.
The Hail Mary at each corner is offered as an existing prayer, not a new one.

Editor: the pilgrim use of the psalms is now framed as tradition ('tradition hears some of the Psalms as songs for pilgrims'), not as a fact; 'what Catholics believe' changed to 'what the Catechism says', matching the cited CCC 2691.
